text: You already covered standard WITH CTE syntax back in Chapter Four, and PostgreSQL uses exactly that syntax, with zero changes needed. High value customers as a CTE, joined to a customers table — nothing new here. This lesson goes deeper into PostgreSQL-specific behavior around that syntax, not the syntax itself.

Here's the real gotcha, historically. Before PostgreSQL version twelve, every single CTE was always materialized — run fully, stored, then used by the outer query — never inlined into the outer query's plan the way a subquery would be. This is called being an optimization fence, and on older PostgreSQL, it could make a CTE noticeably slower than the equivalent subquery, with identical SQL text.

PostgreSQL twelve changed the default. A non-recursive CTE is now inlined automatically, just like a subquery, unless you explicitly mark it MATERIALIZED. If you specifically want the old fenced behavior back — maybe the CTE has a side effect, or you want to stabilize a plan — you add MATERIALIZED yourself.

Knowing which PostgreSQL version you're running actually matters here, in a way it simply doesn't for the rest of standard CTE syntax. The exact same query can behave as optimized-like-a-subquery on one version, and always-fully-materialized-first on another.

And recursive CTEs need one more thing: WITH RECURSIVE, explicitly. T-SQL and Oracle infer the recursion automatically from a CTE referencing itself. PostgreSQL requires the RECURSIVE keyword — the same requirement MySQL has, and different from T-SQL and Oracle.

So: syntax unchanged from Chapter Four, materialization behavior that depends on your PostgreSQL version, and WITH RECURSIVE required for self-reference. Next lesson: PostgreSQL's own specific operators — ILIKE, regex matching, and DISTINCT ON. See you there.
